registers.name_in_paper: Danish matched worker-firm-trade data (as used by HJMX 2011)
registers.role: sample frame, treatment (displacement and firm offshoring), controls, linkage

registers.name_in_paper: central registers of individual training histories
registers.role: outcomes (completion of vocational, postsecondary and basic training courses)

linkages: Training histories recorded at central registers joined to the worker, firm and trade data employed by HJMX 2011
Workers linked to firms, and firms to their trade (import) flows, through the matched worker-firm-trade data
Workers tracked over time regardless of employment status or employer identity, which is what permits the transition analysis

sample.universe: Danish manufacturing workers employed at large importing firms, observed in the registers throughout 1995–2006
selection_rules: All workers must be observed throughout 1995–2006 (a worker is not observed if he or she dies or migrates out of Denmark)
All workers are manufacturing workers who, in at least one of the years 1997–2000, are full-time employed by a firm that imports at least DKK 600,000 and has at least 50 employees
Mass layoff defined as at least 30 percent of the workers employed at time t−1 no longer employed by the firm at time t
A worker is classified as an 'offshorer' if his/her employer increased predicted offshoring by at least 10 percent from year t−1 to t
One third of displaced or affected workers have no observed change in predicted offshoring (missing instruments for some firms, and some predisplacement firms closed down) and so cannot be classified

construction_notes: The dependent variable P_is is a dummy equal to 1 if worker i completes a training program in year s; Figure 1 reports vocational training

Training courses are grouped into basic, vocational and postsecondary; vocational courses last two to three weeks, require employer sponsorship, take place during work hours, and account for 77 percent of government training expenditures
Predicted offshoring is taken from HJMX 2011 and is meant to capture changes due to foreign supply shocks rather than firm-endogenous technological change
The event-time window runs from t−3 to t+3 around the mass-layoff year t; the event year t varies across firms and workers
The omitted/baseline category is the residual group of all workers not employed by the mass-layoff firms
Controls x_is: union, marriage, education status, firm size, and a routineness measure of the worker's occupation

Approximately 9 percent of workers are displaced in a mass-layoff event at least once over 1998–2006 and 33 percent remain employed with the mass-layoff firms; of the two-thirds of displaced or affected workers with an observed change in predicted offshoring, roughly 25 percent are classified as offshorers

Labor-market status after displacement is classified into four categories: without employment (unemployed or out of the work force), and employment with public plus primary (agricultural), service, or manufacturing sectors
'Trained' in the transition analysis means the worker completed vocational training in year t−1

claims.statement: Workers displaced in a mass layoff from a firm that substantially increased offshoring take up vocational training at a 7 percentage point higher rate than the baseline population in the year of displacement.

treatment.label: displaced offshorer (DO): laid off in a mass layoff from a firm whose predicted offshoring rose by at least 10 percent from t−1 to t

definition.value: Worker laid off in a mass-layoff event (at least 30 percent of the workers employed at t−1 no longer employed by the firm at t) at a firm classified as an “offshorer”, i.e. one whose predicted offshoring rose by at least 10 percent from t−1 to t. Predicted offshoring is taken from HJMX 2011 and reflects foreign supply shocks.

timing.value: Group membership is fixed at the mass-layoff event year t; the firm's offshoring increase is measured from t−1 to t.

definition.value: A dummy equal to 1 if the worker completes a (vocational) training program in year s. Vocational courses last two to three weeks, typically require employer sponsorship and take place during work hours; they represent most training activity in Denmark and 77 percent of government training expenditures. Figure 1 plots the vocational-training take-up rate difference relative to the baseline (residual) population.

timing.value: Measured in event year t relative to the mass-layoff year t; Figure 1 plots coefficients for the seven event years t−3 through t+3.

units.value: difference in the probability of completing a vocational training program in the year, relative to the baseline population of workers not employed by mass-layoff firms (0.07 = 7 percentage points)

magnitude.interpretation: a training rate 36 percent higher than the rest of the population

estimand.target_population: Workers in the estimation sample belonging to this group; the coefficient is the group's difference in take-up from the residual population of workers not employed by mass-layoff firms, conditional on α_i, α_s and x_is.
estimand.time_horizon: event year t relative to the mass-layoff year t

population.description: Danish manufacturing workers observed continuously 1995–2006 who were, in at least one of 1997–2000, full-time employed by a firm importing at least DKK 600,000 and with at least 50 employees; 116,190 workers and 1.39 million worker-year observations. The regression sample contains both the four mass-layoff groups and the residual baseline population.

definition.value: Worker who remains employed with the mass-layoff firm, where that firm is classified as an “offshorer” (predicted offshoring rose by at least 10 percent from t−1 to t).

timing.value: Group membership is fixed at the mass-layoff event year t; the firm's offshoring increase is measured from t−1 to t.

definition.value: A dummy equal to 1 if the worker completes a (vocational) training program in year s. Vocational courses last two to three weeks, typically require employer sponsorship and take place during work hours; they represent most training activity in Denmark and 77 percent of government training expenditures. Figure 1 plots the vocational-training take-up rate difference relative to the baseline (residual) population.

timing.value: Measured in event year t+1 relative to the mass-layoff year t; Figure 1 plots coefficients for the seven event years t−3 through t+3.

units.value: difference in the probability of completing a vocational training program in the year, relative to the baseline population of workers not employed by mass-layoff firms, as plotted on the Figure 1 y-axis (a proportion; 0.02 per gridline)

magnitude.interpretation: an increase of over 6 percent in years t and t + 1

estimand.target_population: Workers in the estimation sample belonging to this group; the coefficient is the group's difference in take-up from the residual population of workers not employed by mass-layoff firms, conditional on α_i, α_s and x_is.
estimand.time_horizon: event year t+1 relative to the mass-layoff year t

population.description: Danish manufacturing workers observed continuously 1995–2006 who were, in at least one of 1997–2000, full-time employed by a firm importing at least DKK 600,000 and with at least 50 employees; 116,190 workers and 1.39 million worker-year observations. The regression sample contains both the four mass-layoff groups and the residual baseline population.
subgroups_defined: residual category: workers not employed by mass-layoff firms
population.selection: Workers must be observed in the register throughout 1995–2006 (a worker is not observed if he or she dies or migrates out of Denmark) and must have been full-time employed at a large manufacturing importer in at least one of 1997–2000. One third of displaced or affected workers have no observed change in predicted offshoring and so cannot be classified.

identification.source_of_variation: Firm-level mass-layoff events (1998–2006) combined with firm-level increases in predicted offshoring between t−1 and t, where predicted offshoring is taken from HJMX 2011 and is driven by foreign supply shocks.

key_assumptions.assumption: Mass layoffs (at least 30 percent of a firm's t−1 workforce gone by t) identify genuine displacement rather than voluntary quits, so the displaced groups are not self-selected leavers.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted by analogy to Jacobson, LaLonde and Sullivan (1993); no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Predicted offshoring captures changes in offshoring driven by exogenous foreign supply shocks rather than by technological change endogenous to the firm, so the offshorer/nonoffshorer split is not driven by firm technology.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; the predicted-offshoring measure is taken from HJMX 2011 and is not re-validated here.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on worker fixed effects, year fixed effects and time-varying worker characteristics, membership of a group-by-event-time cell is unrelated to the remaining determinants of training take-up, so δ_k measures the group's difference from the baseline population.

rhs: unobserved determinants of training take-up ε_is

implies_edges.from: mass layoff / offshoring at other firms
implies_edges.to: vocational-training take-up of the residual (baseline) workers

threats_discussed: Anticipation: workers or firms foreseeing the mass layoff and the offshoring episode two years ahead
